definitions.name: Transaction
definitions.description:
Shows and closes the record Mercury keeps of your work in this project. Optional: use it when the task wants a checked finish, or to see what has changed and what was checked.

You never write to the record. Every change a tool lands in this project (Edit, Write, ChangeSet, AstEdit, NotebookEdit, LSP writes, Structure, …) and every check that runs (tests, builds, type checks and lints run through Bash; Test, Launch and Journey runs) is recorded as it happens. Where Mercury finds no test or build setup, reading each changed file back in full counts as the check. A record starts with the first change after the last finish.

{ op: "status" } — what changed, which checks ran after the last change, and whether "completed" can land now.
{ op: "finish", verdict, unresolved? } — closes and saves the record. "completed" lands only when a check ran after the last change, the newest such check passed, and no change attempted after it failed or ended indeterminate; otherwise it is refused, the refusal names what is missing, and the record stays open. "failed" and "abandoned" always land. Put real remaining doubt in unresolved; it is kept word for word.

op.description: status: what changed, which checks ran since the last change, whether "completed" can land · finish: close and save the record

verdict.description: finish (required there): "completed" is refused until a check after the last change passed; "failed" and "abandoned" always land

unresolved.description: finish: real remaining doubt, kept word for word on the record

definitions.name: Structure
definitions.description:
Structural queries by node kind, and previewed, stale-safe codemods, over JS/TS/JSX/TSX only, on the TypeScript compiler's syntax tree. To find code by its shape in any language use AstSearch, and AstEdit to rewrite every match; use this tool for JS/TS questions by node kind — imports by module, calls by dotted callee, declarations by kind and name, a node inside a named class or function — and for a rename, import swap, callee swap or property value that must land as one previewed change.

1. op:"query" (select, filters…) — a bounded AST query. Selects: function · class · interface · type-alias · enum · method · variable · call · import · export · property · string · jsx-element. Filters: name (exact or glob with *), callee ('fs.*'), module, value, within ('class:Name'), files (globs relative to the project root), limit (default 50, max 200). Only .js .jsx .mjs .cjs .ts .mts .cts .tsx files are read. Returns stable match ids (sm-…) and the record mercury://structure/query/<id>.
2. op:"preview" (action, queryId?, matchIds?) — writes nothing; shows the files, the match count and each edit's first line before and after (8 per file, the rest counted). Actions: replace (replacement; $TEXT is the original node) · rename (to — the name token only) · remove · insert-before/insert-after (replacement — new text on its own line at the node's boundary) · replace-import (newModule) · replace-callee (to) · set-value (newValue).
3. op:"apply" (previewId) — refuses if a file changed since the preview or the result would not parse; writes atomically with rollback, verifies by re-reading, reruns parse diagnostics, and reports a partial application as a failure.
4. op:"explain" (matchId, queryId?) — the AST ancestry of one match.

Records: mercury://structure/query/<id> · mercury://structure/preview/<id> (Inspect).

select.description: query: what to select (function · class · call · import · property · …)

name.description: query: name filter — exact or glob with *

callee.description: query select:call — dotted callee glob (console.log · fs.* · *.push)

files.description: query: file globs relative to the project root

queryId.description: preview/explain: the query record (sq-…); defaults to the latest

replacement.description: preview replace · insert-before · insert-after: the new text ($TEXT, in replace, is the original node)

newModule.description: preview replace-import: the new module specifier

newValue.description: preview set-value: the new property value text

definitions.name: AstSearch
definitions.description:
Use this over Grep to find code by its shape rather than its text: a pattern written as code in the target language, with meta-variables for the parts that vary, is matched against each file's parsed syntax tree, so strings and comments never match.

Patterns:
- One complete node, written as code: a call "$FN($$$ARGS)", a statement "if ($COND) { $$$BODY }", an import "import { $$$NAMES } from '$MODULE'". Wrap a fragment that is not standalone in its container: "class $_ { $$$BODY }".
- $NAME matches one node and captures it; $$$NAME matches zero or more siblings (arguments, parameters, statements) and captures them; $_ and $$$ match without capturing. Names are UPPERCASE letters, digits and _; a name used twice must match identical code; $$X and $$$name are literal text. Spacing, line breaks and comments never matter.
- A symbol by name is its declaration, written with every part it has: "function process_order($$$ARGS) { $$$BODY }", "def process_order($$$ARGS): $$$BODY"; a declared return type needs ": $_" (TypeScript) or " -> $_" (Python) after the parameters.

Scope and results:
- path is a file or a directory (the working directory when omitted); glob narrows it, relative to path: "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.py", and {a,b} for alternatives: "**/*.{ts,tsx}". The walk skips dot-files, dot-folders, node_modules, dist, build, out, coverage, venv, __pycache__, vendor, target and the root .gitignore's plain entries; name such a folder in path to search it.
- Each file's language comes from its extension — this build carries: python · go · rust · javascript · typescript · tsx · bash · c-sharp · cpp · css · java · php · ruby · powershell · ini · regex; lang keeps only that language (and forces it on a single file). A file with no grammar is skipped and counted, a file that does not parse is reported, and neither is ever matched.
- Matches come in file order as file:line:col with the code and every capture, limit at a time (default 50, max 200), the rest counted — page with offset; mode "count" tallies per file. AstEdit rewrites exactly the matches this tool finds.

pattern.description: The structural pattern: code in the target language with meta-variables — $NAME for one node, $$$NAME for a sequence, e.g. "$FN($$$ARGS)" or "if ($COND) { $$$BODY }"

path.description: Where to search — a file or a directory; the current working directory when omitted.

glob.description: Restrict the search to files matching this glob, relative to path, e.g. "**/*.ts" or "src/**/*.py"; {a,b} lists alternatives: "**/*.{ts,tsx}"

lang.description: Force one language instead of detecting it per file from the extension (typescript, python, go, rust, …)

mode.description: "matches" (the default) lists each match with its captures; "count" tallies matches per file

limit.description: Matches to return (default 50, max 200); the rest is counted, never dropped silently.

offset.description: Matches to skip before the window (paging). Default 0.

definitions.name: AstEdit
definitions.description:
Use this over Edit to rewrite every match of a code shape at once, across files, as one reviewed change: each match of a structural pattern is replaced by a rewrite built from its captures.

- Patterns, path, glob ({a,b} for alternatives) and lang work as in AstSearch, which finds exactly the matches this tool rewrites — search first when unsure what will change.
- The rewrite is code in the target language: $NAME and $$$NAME insert the captured source verbatim; "" deletes the matched node (a node that owns its line takes the line with it). Every meta-variable in the rewrite must be captured by the pattern; $_ and $$$ cannot be inserted.
- Two calls, always: first without apply — the unified diff per file and a plan "ae-…", nothing written; then the same arguments with apply: true and that plan. Apply refuses, writing nothing, when a file, the pattern, the rewrite or the scope differs from that dry run: run the dry run again and use its plan. Apply writes through the edit permission ask, with /rewind snapshots, atomic writes with rollback, re-read verification and one change receipt, and names each file's fresh anchor.
- Refused by name, nothing written: a match nested inside another (narrow the pattern or the scope), a result that would not parse, a rewrite naming an uncaptured meta-variable, more than 100 files or 500 matches. To change only some matches, put the code that tells them apart into the pattern, or narrow path or glob.
- For a one-off textual change, Edit is the better tool.

pattern.description: The structural pattern to match — code in the target language with $NAME (one node) and $$$NAME (a sequence) meta-variables

rewrite.description: The replacement, as code; $NAME and $$$NAME insert the captured source. "" deletes each matched node.

path.description: Where to rewrite — a file or a directory; the current working directory when omitted.

glob.description: Restrict to files matching this glob, relative to path, e.g. "**/*.ts"; {a,b} lists alternatives: "**/*.{ts,tsx}"

lang.description: Force one language instead of detecting it per file from the extension

apply.description: Omitted or false: a dry run — the diff and a plan token, nothing written. true: write the change; needs plan from the dry run.

plan.description: The plan token (ae-…) the dry run returned; apply refuses when anything differs from that dry run.

definitions.name: ChangeSet
definitions.description:
Use this over Edit when the same change spans several files: one coordinated review and apply.

Atomic multi-file text change sets: one call prepares, reviews, and applies an anchored change spanning several existing text files, with all-target preflight before the first write, one aggregate operator decision, drift refusal per target, deterministic journaled recovery, and exact outcome truth.

Operations:
1. { op: "apply", changes: [...] } — the fast path: preflight every member, obtain one aggregate decision, apply. Use this when you already hold fresh Read anchors for every file.
2. { op: "preview", changes: [...] } — the review path: build an immutable content-addressed plan (cs-…) and write nothing. Then { op: "apply", plan_id: "cs-…" }. A drifted file refuses the whole apply and names the Read that refreshes its anchor.
3. { op: "status", plan_id } — plan state + per-file freshness.
4. { op: "discard", plan_id } — retire a prepared plan.

Each changes[] member targets one existing text file with the Edit vocabulary:
  { file_path, expected_anchor (required — the "(anchor: …)" value from your Read), hunks: [{ lines: "N" | "N-M", replace, insert?: "before"|"after" }] or edits: [{ old_string, new_string, replace_all? }], op?: "edit" | "delete" | "move", new_path? }
Hunks are 1-based against the anchored snapshot and must be disjoint; "" deletes the range; insert takes a single anchor line. Edits match the same snapshot, each old_string occurring once unless replace_all, and must address disjoint text; a member carries hunks or edits, not both. op "delete" removes the file (neither); op "move" renames it to new_path, which must not exist, after any hunks or edits. A file's read knowledge is keyed to its content: a Read of the lines the edit touches, a content-mode Grep that displayed them, or expected_anchor from a full Read all count.

The contract:
· any preparation/validation/scope/drift failure writes nothing — the valid subset of an invalid set is never applied;
· a normal apply reaches the complete planned state, verified by reread;
· a midway interruption is journaled and deterministically reconciled at the next boot;
· if later bytes prevent safe reconciliation, the exact unresolved paths are named — uncertainty is never reported as success.

Already-satisfied members are not failures: they are omitted from writes and reported as noChangePaths. An all-satisfied set returns one truthful no-change result with zero writes. Applying an already-committed plan replays the prior result without writing twice.

Bounds (an exceeded bound names the limit and the smallest recovery): 16 files/set · 32 hunks/file · 128 hunks/set · 4MB staged content/set · 16 retained plans · 30-minute plan lifetime.

Not this tool (refused by name): file creation (Write) · binary content · notebooks (NotebookEdit) · command execution (Bash).

changes.description: preview / apply: the file members (one per existing text file)

file_path.description: Absolute path to an EXISTING text file

expected_anchor.description: REQUIRED staleness anchor from a prior Read of this file (the "(anchor: …)" value)

hunks.description: Disjoint line-addressed hunks against the anchored snapshot (the Edit hunk vocabulary); an edit member (op "edit", the default) carries hunks or edits, a move optionally, a delete neither

lines.description: 1-based original line ("12") or inclusive range ("12-18") of the anchored snapshot

replace.description: Replacement body ("" deletes the range; with insert, the inserted body)

insert.description: Insert relative to the single anchor line instead of replacing it

edits.description: Exact-string edits against the anchored snapshot (the Edit old_string/new_string vocabulary), instead of hunks; each old_string must occur once unless replace_all

old_string.description: The text to replace, as the file spells it

new_string.description: The text to replace it with ("" deletes the text)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

op.description: "edit" (default) applies the hunks or edits; "delete" removes the file (neither); "move" renames it to new_path after any hunks or edits

new_path.description: move: the absolute destination path, which must not exist

plan_id.description: apply / status / discard: a plan id (cs-…) from a prior preview

definitions.name: Git
definitions.description:
An optional typed surface for local status, diffs, staging and explicitly requested preview-first commit plans; the repository commit workflow uses Bash, and this surface is for work that should be inspectable and verifiable. It never pushes, never fetches, never rewrites history, never discards uncommitted content.

Where it runs: cwd (optional) names the folder; the session folder when absent. The repository containing that folder is used, or the one repository directly below it. A folder with no repository, or with several directly below it, is refused — pass cwd:"<one of them>".

Observation (free):
- op:"status" — branch · changed files · the tree digest plans pin to. mercury://git/status
- op:"diff" (scope: worktree|staged|commit|range, ref?, paths?) — bounded files + hunks with stable ids (gh-…) for exact staging.
- op:"show" (sha) · op:"worktree" · op:"conflicts" (three-way heads) · op:"mergebase" (refA, refB).
- op:"fileAtRef" (ref, path) — one file's content at an exact ref (full payload: mercury://git/at/<ref>/<path>). op:"tree" (ref, path?) — one directory level at a ref. op:"compare" (refA=base, refB=head) — ahead/behind counts + bounded commit lists + three-dot diffstat.

Commit plans:
- op:"plan" (groups: [{files, hunks?, message, checks?}]) — a preview-first atomic plan: validates every file really changed, no file in two groups, names exclusions and ambiguous (staged+unstaged) files, pins the tree digest; it commits nothing. mercury://git/plan/<id>
- op:"apply" (planId) — revalidates the digest (a changed tree refuses: stale plan), then per group stages exactly the planned files/hunks, commits, and verifies the created commit's file list from the commit itself. A failure mid-plan stops there: created commits stand, content is never lost.
- op:"verify" (planId) — is the plan still applicable / what did it create?

Index operations (asked):
- op:"stage" (files, hunks?) — exact file/hunk staging. op:"restore" (files) — index-only unstage, working copy untouched. op:"resolve" (path, take:ours|theirs or content) — resolve + stage a conflict.

Review (observational; push/comment stay with explicit workflows):
- op:"reviewContext" (pr?) — the composed review input: the reviewed diff set (worktree or PR) + the project-intel impact ref + an honest diagnostics note. mercury://repo/review/context
- op:"reviewRecord" (findings, inspected, reviewNote?, pr?) — record a typed review: class defect|question|polish · severity · exact path+range inside the reviewed set (locations are never invented); an empty review must name what it inspected. mercury://repo/review/latest
- repository-host context (read-only, via the gh session): mercury://repo · /branch · /pr/<n> · /checks/<n> · /issue/<n> — read them with Read or Inspect.

Host observation (read-only, never publishes/pushes; MERCURY_REPO_HOST):
- op:"hostSearch" (searchKind: code|commits|prs|issues, query, limit?) — bounded typed host search.
- op:"prDiff" (pr?, file?, page?) — the PR's changed-file list, or one file's diff a page at a time (80 lines/page). mercury://repo/pr/<n>/diff
- op:"runs" (limit? · run?) — workflow-run list, or one run with its jobs. mercury://repo/runs
- op:"runWatch" (run, cancel?) — a cancellable watch on one run (returns immediately; settles from the observed conclusion).

cwd.description: the folder to run in (default: the session folder). The repository containing it is used; when it is not inside one but holds exactly one repository directly below it, that one is used

groups.description: plan: the proposed commit groups, in dependency order

files.description: exact repo-relative paths (a file belongs to at most one group)

hunks.description: optional per-file exact hunk-id subsets (gh-… from op:"diff")

message.description: the commit message for this group

checks.description: checks associated with this group (recorded on the plan)

content.description: resolve: explicit resolved content (instead of take)

pr.description: reviewContext/prDiff: compose against this PR instead of the current branch (needs the gh session)

findings.description: reviewRecord: the typed findings (empty = an honest no-findings review; inspected required)

class.description: verified defect · open question · non-blocking polish

path.description: exact repo-relative path inside the reviewed diff set

inspected.description: reviewRecord: what was actually inspected (required when findings is empty)

searchKind.description: hostSearch: what to search on the host

query.description: hostSearch: the search query (GitHub search syntax)

limit.description: hostSearch/runs: result bound (search ≤50 default 10 · runs ≤20 default 10)

file.description: prDiff: one changed file's path — pages that file's diff (omit for the file list)

page.description: prDiff: 0-based page of the selected file (80 diff lines per page)

run.description: runs/runWatch: a workflow-run id (runs: inspect one run · runWatch: the run to watch)

cancel.description: runWatch: true cancels the live watch for `run` instead of starting one

definitions.name: Journey

op.description: run a journey · status of one · list recorded

definitions.name: Browser
definitions.description:
Drive a real browser through the bundled driver: one owned headless session per agent (launched on first open, reaped on close/exit — concurrent agents each drive their own, they never share a page), full provenance on every act.

op:"status" — the resolution verdict (operator pin > managed Chrome-for-Testing cache > unavailable; installed browsers are discovered for information and never driven), driver/browser versions, the live-session state, the session's approved origins and the approval rule; never launches a browser session.
op:"open" (url, waitUntil?, timeoutMs?) — navigate to an http(s) URL (settles on load by default — networkidle2 for busy SPAs, domcontentloaded for speed; timeoutMs reaches 90s for a cold dev-server compile). A page census of 0 body-text chars means the app is still rendering: waitFor a selector or text before extract/screenshot.
op:"click" (selector, or x+y) — click an element or a viewport point. Selector clicks auto-wait (present and visible, bounded by timeoutMs) and gate on actionability: a disabled or covered target refuses instead of clicking nowhere. After a click that starts a navigation, op:"waitFor" (navigation) lets it settle.
op:"type" (text, selector?, clear?, enter?) — type into the selector-named element (auto-waited, focused first, shadow roots resolved) or the currently focused element. Only text-bearing targets accept text (text/search/url/tel/email/number/date-family inputs, textarea, contenteditable); checkboxes/radios/buttons, file inputs and readOnly fields refuse. Credential-shaped fields (password inputs, one-time-code/cc-* autocomplete, password/otp/secret/api-key-shaped names) refuse plain text; the one road into a credential field is secretRef: the operator registers a named secret out-of-band (a MERCURY_BROWSER_SECRET_<NAME> env var, or the browser-secrets file in the config home, owner-only mode) and op:"type" with secretRef:"NAME" + selector fills it — the value never enters this conversation, the fill lands only on credential-shaped targets, and the operator approves the secret + origin pairing (an approved origin alone never covers it).
op:"scroll" (selector, or dy) — scroll an element into view, or by dy pixels (positive = down).
op:"waitFor" (selector | text | neither = navigation; state?, timeoutMs?) — event-driven waiting bounded by a deadline (default 10000ms, cap 30000ms). Selector waits default to visible (a pre-rendered hidden modal is not "present"); state chooses attached or hidden instead. Text waits match case-insensitively with whitespace normalized. A navigation wait whose navigation already landed during the previous act returns at once. Prefer this over any fixed pause.
op:"back" / op:"reload" — history navigation / reload the current page.
op:"select" (selector, values) — choose <select> options by value, falling back to visible label. A native dropdown cannot be driven by click; select drives it.
op:"press" (key, modifiers?) — press a navigation or edit key (Enter, Escape, Tab, arrows, Backspace, Delete, Home/End, PageUp/PageDown). Printable characters are deliberately not pressable — type owns them, and refuses credential fields.
op:"hover" (selector) — hover an element (menus and controls that render on hover).
op:"viewport" (width, height, deviceScaleFactor?) — resize the render surface (session default 1280x800 desktop). A read — no origin ask.
op:"extract" (mode: "text"|"tree", selector?, offset?) — the page as readable text (innerText) or as an accessibility-tree projection (indented role "name" [state] lines; the tree includes iframe content — selectors do not reach into frames). Output beyond 15000 chars is truncated — offset pages the window, selector narrows the scope.
op:"console" (limit?) — the page's bounded truth ring (last 250 entries, newest last): console logs, page errors with their stack head, network failures and 4xx/5xx responses (method + path + status), navigation dividers, and dialogs. "why is this page broken" reads from here. JS dialogs are auto-dismissed (beforeunload auto-accepted) and land in the ring with their text; choosing a dialog's answer is not offered.
op:"info" — current URL, title and the origin's approval state; cheap facts, no side effects.
op:"screenshot" (fullPage?, selector?, label?) — capture the page, the full scroll height, or one element (selector) to a PNG artifact; the image is attached to the result only when your engine takes image input, else the result names the file.
op:"close" — end the session (origin approvals die with it). Every op is bounded: a browser that stops answering is given 90s per protocol call and close 3s before its process is ended.

Selectors: every selector door takes CSS by default, plus four forms the bundled driver resolves everywhere: aria/<name>[role="<role>"] (role + the exact full accessible name — the two fields extract mode:"tree" prints, so a tree line `button "Save"` is addressable as aria/Save[role="button"]), text/<substring> (substring of rendered text), xpath/<expr>, and the >>> deep combinator that pierces shadow roots (my-widget >>> input). Read with extract mode:"tree", then act with the selector the tree handed you — never guess a CSS class on an app you have not read.

Auto-wait: selector acts (click/type/scroll) resolve with a bounded present-and-visible wait (default 10000ms, cap 30000ms, timeoutMs overrides) — a late-rendered element needs no waitFor first. Scoped reads (extract selector) wait for attached only — hidden content is readable, not actable.

A click that opens a new tab closes it unadopted (one owned page) — op:"open" its URL to follow it.

Permissions: the first visit to an origin asks the operator by URL; once approved, opening and acting anywhere on that origin rides the grant for the rest of the session. A navigation that crosses to an unapproved origin (a link click, a redirect) re-asks before the next act there. Reads (status/waitFor/extract/console/info/screenshot) never ask — on a crossed-to origin too, so an approved page can lead you to read pages elsewhere: name the origin when you report them, and know the operator approved only the origin they were asked for. Sessions and origin approvals are per agent: an approval granted in one agent's session never authorizes another agent, and concurrent browser children are capped (close another session, or the operator raises MERCURY_BROWSER_MAX_SESSIONS). A secret fill (type + secretRef) is its own consent class, approved per secret + origin pairing for the session.

Downloads are never implicit: the driven session denies page-initiated downloads at the protocol level and the result names what was refused — "the link is a download (<type>, <size>, saves as <name>)" on a click, "open failed: <url> is a download (…)" on an open — downloads are not followed here; fetch the file with WebFetch or Bash instead; the one consented download road is provisioning the engine itself — op:"provision" (buildId?) asks the operator before installing a Chrome-for-Testing build (/browser install is the same road by hand). When nothing resolves, provision instead of dead-ending or hand-rolling a headless-Chrome harness. File uploads stay out of scope. The driver needs node >= 22.12.

definitions.name: Computer
definitions.description:
Call Computer directly, not through Eval. Coordinates are pixels of its last screenshot; renew after compaction/frame changes. target:{role?,name?,text?,nth?}: exact role/name, text substring; nth selects a 1-based match.
screenshot: front window; full:true/display:N for a display. region:{x,y,width,height} uses last-shot pixels. scale:0.25–1 (window .5, display/region 1). These capture options also work on acts with capture:true.
Terminal screenshot/tree reads AX text, cut at 15000; pixels:true gets an image.
click(x,y OR target OR ref,count? 1–3,modifiers?) · doubleClick · rightClick · move. drag adds toX/toY OR toTarget; scroll adds dx/dy notches, positive down/right.
type(text) ≤4000, newline/tab only controls. key(key); hold(key,durationMs) 50–5000ms. Keys: Enter, Escape, Tab, Space, Backspace, Delete, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, ArrowUp/Down/Left/Right, F1–F12 or one character, with cmd/ctrl/alt/shift joined by +.
tree: [n] role "title" value; ref:n until reread. root:n|{role,name}; all:true hidden; points:true pixels. Depth/rows 12/400, caps 32/2000, larger budgets clamp; scope:window default, app includes menus/windows; find(target). Targets use caps by default.
wait(durationMs?,until?) 1000 default/10000 max: until:{text}, {role,name}, {title} or {url} (substrings); gone:true waits for an element to leave. Image on match/capture:true; capture:false overrides. cursor/displays/frontmost read facts.
read(target|ref) returns labelled text/value, up to 20000 chars; clipboard:true reads copied text with separate consent. focusApp:{name} brings a running app forward (name or bundle id).
sequence(steps): acts/reads/screenshot, no nesting; first failure stops. Screenshot steps capture there; one final image unless capture:false. Put capture/region/scale/settleMs on the sequence.
Acts: image only with capture:true; label?; verify:true compares trees, not task success. settleMs 300/5000 max; changed/unchanged tracks title/focus, not page readiness; use wait-until for readiness.
After the same act twice with an unchanged result, read the screen before acting again.
The first act in an application asks; tree/find/read/wait-until share its grant. Other reads never ask. Sovereign skips asks. One driving session. Own terminal: only app-switch keys or focusApp; clicks outside its window. esc/ctrl+c releases input. Operator typing pauses/refuses acts. Never solve captchas: captcha:true hands them to the operator. Screenshots leave saved history.

definitions.name: EnterWorktree
definitions.description:
Split off an isolated git worktree and move this session into it.

## When it applies
Only on the word "worktree" from the user — "work in a worktree", "make a worktree for this", "do it in a separate worktree"; never for branch work or ordinary feature or bugfix work, however large.

## Requirements
- A git repository.
- The session is not already in a worktree it created.

## Behaviour
Inside a repository, a new worktree is created under the project config home's worktrees directory (`.mercury/worktrees/`) on a new branch based on the current head. Outside one, the configured hooks provide VCS-agnostic isolation. The session's working directory switches into the worktree. Leave mid-session with the exit tool (keep-or-remove choice); ending the session also prompts.

## Parameters
- `name` (optional): the worktree name. Within each slash-delimited segment the permitted characters are letters, digits, and the dot/underscore/dash trio; the whole name may not exceed 64 characters. Omitted, a random name is generated.

name.description: Worktree name: letters, digits, dots, underscores, and dashes within each slash-delimited segment; at most 64 characters. Omitted ⇒ a generated name.

definitions.name: ExitWorktree
definitions.description:
Ends a worktree session that was started with the EnterWorktree tool and returns the session to the original directory.

Scope — this tool does not touch a worktree created by hand (git worktree add, scripts, other tools), one the EnterWorktree tool created in a previous session, or the current directory when EnterWorktree was never called this session: outside an active worktree session the call answers that no session is active and touches no files.

When to use: only on the user's explicit ask to exit or leave the worktree, or to return to the original directory.

Parameters:
- action: "keep" preserves the worktree directory and branch on disk — use it when the user may return to the work or has changes worth preserving. "remove" deletes both the directory and the branch — the clean exit for finished or abandoned work.
- discard_changes (default false): only meaningful with action "remove". It must be true when uncommitted files or unmerged commits sit in the worktree; otherwise the tool refuses and lists what it found. Get the user's word before re-invoking with discard_changes: true.

Behavior:
- The session's working directory is restored to the original directory.
- Caches that depend on the working directory are cleared.
- A tmux session attached to the worktree is killed on "remove"; on "keep" it keeps running, its name coming back for the user to reattach.
- EnterWorktree can be called again afterwards to start a new worktree session.

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree directory and its branch on disk for later; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required to be true when removing a worktree that has uncommitted files or unmerged commits; without it the tool refuses and lists them.

definitions.name: Checkpoint
definitions.description:
Use this with Rewind for a detour you don't want to keep in context: mark the state before you start.

Mark the current conversation state as a checkpoint before starting an exploratory detour (a risky refactor investigation, a speculative design probe, a large read-heavy dig) whose transcript you may not want to keep in context afterwards.

- State the goal of the exploration in `goal` — it is echoed back on Rewind.
- One checkpoint may be active at a time; a second call refuses (typed) until you Rewind.
- While a checkpoint is active, ending the run without Rewind gets a settle warning: either Rewind with a report, or say explicitly why the exploration should stand.
- Rewind restores the model context only: your files, git state, and the operator's visible transcript are never touched by this pair. (The operator's own /rewind command is a different device and can restore code.)
- After Rewind, everything between the checkpoint and the rewind disappears from your context; your `report` is retained as the one carried-back artifact. Write it like a handoff: findings, decisions, exact paths.

goal.description: What the exploration sets out to learn or attempt — echoed back on Rewind.

definitions.name: Rewind
definitions.description:
Use this with Checkpoint to drop a detour you don't want to keep in context, carrying back only your report.

Restore the model context to the active Checkpoint, abandoning the exploration since it while carrying back your findings.

- `report` is required and non-empty: it is the one artifact that survives the rewind. Write it like a handoff — findings, decisions, exact file paths, next steps.
- The rewind applies at the end of this turn: the next model call sees the pre-exploration context plus your report; everything between checkpoint and rewind leaves the model context.
- The operator's transcript keeps the exploration visible; your files and git state are never touched by this pair.
- Refuses (typed) when no checkpoint is active or the active one was already rewound.

report.description: The carried-back handoff: findings, decisions, exact paths, next steps. Required, non-empty after trim.

definitions.name: SendMessage
definitions.description:
Deliver a message to a running crewmate of this session. It never starts work: a crewmate that has finished is refused, and ResumeCrewmate gives it the message as a new turn.

Example: { "to": "researcher", "message": "The auth notes moved to docs/auth-v2.md; read that one." }

## Addressing
- to: the id a crewmate's launch receipt names, or the name its launch gave it — both reach the same crewmate (a name two launches carried reaches the newest).
- A background crewmate reaches the agent that launched it at "main".

## How communication works
- Plain output reaches no crewmate — words travel only through this tool and ResumeCrewmate.
- A running crewmate reads the message at its next tool boundary, else at the end of its turn. The main agent reads it the same way; between turns it starts a turn for it.
- Content relayed to you is already rendered to the user — do not re-quote it back.

to.description: The crewmate to send to: the id its launch receipt names or the name its launch gave it; "main" from a background crewmate reaches the agent that launched it

definitions.name: ResumeCrewmate
definitions.description:
Give a crewmate of this session more work: your message becomes its next turn. A crewmate that has finished (completed, failed or stopped) is resumed from its transcript in the background, with its full context. A running crewmate is never started twice: it reads the message at its next tool boundary, unless interrupt: true cuts that turn and starts the new one after saving the partial transcript.

Example: { "to": "researcher", "message": "Now map the token refresh path the same way." }

## Addressing
- to: the id a crewmate's launch receipt names, or the name its launch gave it — both reach the same crewmate, running or finished (a name two launches carried reaches the newest).

## Which verb
- ResumeCrewmate when the crewmate must act on the message, running or not; a resumed turn is a paid turn of that crewmate. SendMessage only for a note to a running crewmate. Crewmate starts a new crewmate with no context.
- A resumed crewmate's completion notice reaches the main agent. One launched with output_schema keeps its StructuredOutput tool for the resumed turn.

to.description: The crewmate to resume: the id its launch receipt names or the name its launch gave it

message.description: Its next turn: what to do, written as you would brief it

model.description: Model for the resumed turn of a finished crewmate; omitted, its recorded model stays. Read mercury://models for available ids.

effort.description: Effort for the resumed turn; omitted, its recorded effort stays. Max is admitted; an unsupported lower tier is refused, not clamped.

interrupt.description: Interrupt a running turn and start this message as its next turn; omitted or false, deliver it at the next tool boundary.

definitions.name: Workflow
definitions.description:
Run a JavaScript orchestration script that coordinates a fleet of crewmates with deterministic control flow. The launch detaches immediately: this tool answers with a task ID while the run continues in the background, a <task-notification> arrives at completion, and /workflows shows live progress.

Launching a workflow is the user's choice, never your own judgement that one would help: orchestration can fan out into dozens of billed crewmates, so the scale must be something the user chose. You have that choice only when one of these holds:
- They asked for it in their own words ("run a workflow", "orchestrate this", "fan out crewmates", "use multi-agent"). The words must be theirs; the mere fact that crewmates would speed a task up does not qualify.
- The instructions of a skill or slash command you are executing direct you to invoke Workflow.
- They asked to run a particular saved or built-in workflow by name.

In every other case, keep the tool unused: handle single delegations with one crewmate launch, or describe the workflow you would build, estimate its rough crewmate count and cost, and ask. Mention that the words "use a workflow" next time will grant the opt-in directly.

Every script opens with `export const meta = {...}` as its first statement:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'stale-doc-sweep',
    description: 'Find docs that contradict the code they describe',  // one line; the permission dialog shows it
    phases: [                                                         // mirrors your phase() calls
      { title: 'Inventory', detail: 'pair each doc with its subject module' },
      { title: 'Check', detail: 'one crewmate per pair, quote-level comparison' },
    ],
  }
  // body follows — agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()

`meta` is a pure literal — variables, function calls, spreads, and template interpolation are all rejected. `name` and `description` are required; `whenToUse` (shown when workflows are listed) and `phases` are optional. Phase titles pair with phase() calls by exact string match — a phase() with no meta entry simply opens its own progress group — and a phases entry may carry a `model` field when one phase runs on a specific override.

The script body's hooks:

- agent(prompt, opts?) → Promise<any> — dispatch one crewmate.
  - Return value: the crewmate's closing text as a string; given `schema` (any JSON Schema object) the validated object instead — failed validation makes the crewmate correct itself.
  - Resolves to null in two cases: the user skipped this crewmate mid-run, or it died on an unrecoverable API error after the built-in retries. Fan-out code should `.filter(Boolean)`.
  - opts.label — the display name in progress surfaces (defaults to a prompt prefix).
  - opts.phase — pin this call to a named progress group. Inside pipeline()/parallel() stages always pin explicitly; the ambient phase() pointer is global state and concurrent stages race it. Same string, same group.
  - opts.model — the model for this call, as the operator directs per dispatch: an explicit catalog alias or a declared tier. Accepts anything the session's model catalog resolves: a canonical id, a registered family alias, or — when the operator has a second provider connected — that provider's engine ids. To see the providers the operator is signed into and the models each reaches, read mercury://models and name one of them by its id; a family word runs that family's current default, and when a signed-in provider's live list cannot be read mercury://models/known decides (the family's default this build knows, or an exact id the known page lists). The ladder is live, then known, then web, then ask: read mercury://models, then mercury://models/known. If neither page carries the word, you may use WebSearch with the provider's name and that word, starting with its published models page listed in mercury://models. Web text is unverified: it informs the ask, never a launch. Then ask the operator for the model id with AskUserQuestion, naming the providers that are signed in, the nearest live or known rows, and any web findings with their links; in a headless run say why in one line and stop. Never switch to another provider on your own — if the one you were asked for cannot run, say why and stop. Omitted, the crewmate runs on the session's resolved model.
  - opts.effort — reasoning effort for this call: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max'. Omitted, the configured crewmate default applies (high unless the operator changed it in /config) — never the session's own level. Spend 'low' on mechanical stages; reserve the top tiers for the hardest judge/verify stages (a tier the model's ladder lacks runs the nearest served tier). Setting it also turns on extended reasoning where the model supports it.
  - opts.tier — 'orchestrator' | 'executor': declare the call's role instead of naming a model. A junk tier throws; routing only acts when the operator armed MERCURY_WORKFLOW_ROUTING=1: an 'executor' call with no explicit model then rides the harness's pinned execution-tier model, while 'orchestrator' keeps the session model. A call that names opts.model outranks its tier.
  - opts.isolation: 'worktree' — run in a freshly created git worktree. Costly (worktree setup plus disk per crewmate); use it only when concurrent crewmates would otherwise write the same files. An untouched worktree is removed automatically; a modified one is kept for review.
  - opts.agentType — dispatch a custom crewmate type (say, 'code-reviewer') rather than the built-in workflow worker; its definition's tools: list is followed exactly, as the Crewmate tool would; composable with `schema`.
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...) → Promise<any[]> — push each item through the stage chain independently, with no synchronization between stages: item three can be in its last stage while item seven is still in its first. This is the default engine for multi-stage work — total wall-clock tracks the slowest single item, not the slowest stage times the stage count. Each stage receives (previousResult, originalItem, index). A stage that throws turns that item into null and its remaining stages are skipped.
- parallel(thunks) → Promise<any[]> — run an array of zero-argument functions concurrently and wait for all of them (a barrier). The promise always fulfills: rejected thunks (crewmate deaths included) become null slots in the returned array, so `.filter(Boolean)` before use. Reserve it for a stage that needs the whole previous stage at once — deduplicating across every candidate, an aggregate early exit, prompts that reference sibling results.
- log(message) — one line of narration shown to the user above the run's progress display.
- phase(title) — open a progress group; agent() calls that follow (without opts.phase) attach to it.
- args — the value the Workflow call passed as `args`, verbatim; undefined when absent. Pass real JSON values, never a stringified JSON blob: `args: {targets: ['api', 'cli']}` reaches the script as an object, while a quoted blob arrives as one string and every `args.targets.map`-style access dies.
- budget — {total, spent(), remaining()}: the turn's output-token target when the operator set one. total is null with no target; spent() counts output tokens across the whole turn (main loop plus every workflow — one shared pool); remaining() is max(0, total − spent()), or Infinity when target-less. That target is a hard wall: when spent() crosses total, any later agent() call throws. Loop on remaining() or size a fleet statically: `const LANES = budget.total ? Math.max(2, Math.floor(budget.total / 120_000)) : 4`. Always gate such loops on budget.total — when no target exists, remaining() reads Infinity and nothing stops the loop short of the 1000-agent cap.
- workflow(nameOrRef, args?) → Promise<any> — start a second workflow inline and hand back its result. A string names a saved workflow (the same registry as {name: "..."}); {scriptPath} runs a script file you saved earlier. A child run inherits the parent's agent counter, concurrency ceiling, abort signal, and token pool (its spend lands in budget.spent()). The second argument arrives as the child's `args`. Exactly one level of nesting — a child calling workflow() throws. Unknown names, unreadable paths, and child syntax errors all throw; catch if you want to degrade gracefully.

Agents inside a workflow carry the same tool box as a background crewmate launched by the Crewmate tool — one allow-set, with the spawn, plan and ask surfaces left out — so a model ingests the same tool schemas either way. The built-in worker reaches every session-connected MCP tool through its own tool search, loading schemas on demand; a custom agentType carries exactly the tools its definition declares, as it would under the Crewmate tool. Caveat: MCP servers that authenticate interactively may be unavailable in headless or scheduled runs.

A workflow script is plain JavaScript — TypeScript syntax (annotations like `: string[]`, interfaces, generics) fails the parse. The body executes inside an async wrapper, so await works at the top level. The usual built-ins are present (JSON, Math, Array, ...), with three deliberate holes: Date.now(), Math.random(), and zero-argument new Date() throw, because nondeterminism breaks resume replay. Take timestamps in through args or stamp them after the run returns; get variety by varying prompts/labels with the loop index. The script itself has no filesystem or network — agents do that work.

Limits: at most min(16, CPU cores − 2) agents run at once per workflow (the capacity governor can narrow this further); extra calls queue and start as slots free. Hand parallel()/pipeline() a hundred items freely — they all finish, just not all at once. A single run may make at most 1000 agent() calls (a runaway-loop backstop), and one parallel()/pipeline() call takes at most 4096 items — beyond that throws.

The hooks composed — pipeline by default, verification starting per angle as each review lands:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'api-surface-review',
    description: 'Review public API changes per angle, then check each claim',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Check' }],
  }
  const ANGLES = [{key: 'breaking', brief: '...'}, {key: 'naming', brief: '...'}]
  const checked = await pipeline(
    ANGLES,
    a => agent(a.brief, {label: `review:${a.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: CLAIMS_SCHEMA}),
    out => parallel(out.claims.map(c => () =>
      agent(`Attempt to refute this claim: ${c.text}`, {label: `check:${c.id}`, phase: 'Check', schema: RULING_SCHEMA})
        .then(r => ({...c, ruling: r}))
    ))
  )
  const upheld = checked.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(c => c.ruling?.upheld)
  return { upheld }

## Resume

Every launch reports a runId. After a pause, a kill, or an edit to the script, launch again with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}): agent() calls whose (position, prompt, opts) prefix is unchanged replay instantly from the journal; the first call that differs, plus all calls after it, run live. Unchanged script plus unchanged args replays 100%; changing `args` invalidates the chain on purpose (the input steers the run). If no journal survives, the fallback is manual: read the agent-<id>.jsonl transcripts under the run's transcript directory and write a continuation script from what already finished.

## Mercury workflow authorship doctrine

- Model choice belongs to the operator: name an explicit catalog alias, or a declared tier, for each dispatch — the operator directs models per dispatch. Do not lean on the inherited session model (project-level settings sometimes pin a tier the live session is not using), and never pick an agentType whose definition pins a small-tier model — when you need read-only scoping, put it in the prompt, not in a downgraded engine.
- A verify stage belongs to the workflow's shape itself, never bolted on after: any workflow that performs real implementation (edits, fixes, migrations) carries one — an independent refutation of each claim, or one dedicated checker per changed unit — before it returns success. A fixer crewmate asserting its own success is an assertion, not evidence.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from the project workflows directory). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, never as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script.

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk — the persisted copy an earlier launch named: edit it with Write/Edit and re-invoke with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from (unchanged agent() calls replay from the journal). Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

run_in_background.description: Ignored — workflows always run in the background; the tool returns immediately with a task ID.

definitions.name: Sleep
definitions.description:
Wait out a given duration. An interrupt from the user ends the wait at once, reporting the time actually spent.

Use it when:
- a rest, hold, or break is what the user wants;
- genuinely nothing is actionable right now;
- you are waiting on something outside your control (a long build, an external process, a crewmate's reply) and want to check back later.

While you sleep you may receive periodic check-in prompts wrapped in <tick> tags. Treat each one as a nudge: look for useful work first (unread messages, finished tasks, pending follow-ups) and only go back to sleeping when there is still nothing to do.

Prefer this tool over running `sleep` in the shell: it holds no shell process open, and it can be interrupted cleanly.

Waking is not free. Every wake-up is a model call, and the prompt cache lapses after 5 minutes of idleness, so a longer sleep costs less per unit of time waited while a shorter one reacts sooner.

seconds.description: How many seconds to wait before returning (min 1, max 3600; a value outside the bounds is clamped to them and the result says so). The user can interrupt the sleep at any time (it resolves early, reporting the elapsed time).

definitions.name: CronCreate
definitions.description:
Put a prompt on this session's clock: one run after a delay or at a set time, or a repeating cron schedule. The Mercury daemon keeps it on this session's record and fires it, even into a parked session.

## When: exactly one of
- delayMinutes: "in 20 minutes" → 20.
- at: "3:47pm today" → "<today's date>T15:47". A time already past is refused, never moved to another day.
- cron: never convert to UTC. Fields take numbers, *, ranges (1-5), lists (1,15), steps (*/10); no names (MON, JAN). Every 5 minutes "*/5 * * * *"; hourly at :07 "7 * * * *"; weekdays 09:00 "0 9 * * 1-5".

## The answer
The call waits for the daemon. "Scheduled <id> …" gives the 8-character id and the fire time in local time and UTC: tell the user that time; CronDelete with that id cancels. A refusal means nothing was scheduled; it says why and what to do next. "NOT confirmed" means the request may have landed: check CronList before retrying. "Queued, not confirmed …" means an older daemon took the request without answering: check CronList before telling the user anything is scheduled.

## Firing
- The daemon checks every 30 seconds: a fire lands within 30 seconds after its time, only while the session is idle.
- It runs on this session's model and account. A fire the sign-in cannot serve (expired, rate-limited) is held with a receipt until /logins releases it; a fire due while the machine slept runs late, or past the catch-up window is recorded as missed. Never silently dropped.
- A schedule outlives interrupts; for a self-paced loop that should end when the user interrupts, use ScheduleWakeup (one wake, 1 to 60 minutes).
- At most 50 schedules per session.

## Prompt and title
The prompt comes back verbatim at each fire with no memory of why it was set. Give a title when the user named the task. Mention the /saturn board, where the user sees every schedule.

cron.description: Repeating: 5 fields (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week) in local time, e.g. "0 9 * * 1-5". Pass exactly one of cron, at, delayMinutes.

at.description: One run at a local date and time, "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM" (an offset like "Z" or "+01:00" is accepted); must be in the future.

delayMinutes.description: One run this many minutes from now (1 to 525600); it fires on the next whole minute at or after the delay.

prompt.description: What runs at each fire: self-contained, 1 to 20,000 characters, no secrets (it is stored with the schedule).

recurring.description: With cron only. Default true; false runs once at the next match, then removes itself (for one run prefer at or delayMinutes).

onParked.description: What a fire does when the session is parked: 'wake' (default) reactivates the session and delivers; 'queue' holds the fire for the session's own next wake.

title.description: A short name for the schedule (one line of at most 200 characters), shown on its rows in the chat and the list in place of the id — "morning brief", "nightly audit".

definitions.name: CronDelete
definitions.description: Cancel a schedule on this session's record. Pass the id CronCreate returned or CronList shows. The removal travels on the session's next facts beat and is receipted.

id.description: The schedule id to cancel (eight hex characters — CronList shows them)

definitions.name: CronList
definitions.description: List this session's schedules as the daemon last pushed them: id, human-readable timing, one-shot or recurring, fire-into-session or session-birth, next fire, paused state. A schedule CronCreate answered "Scheduled" is listed already; one it answered "Queued, not confirmed" appears once the daemon applies it.

definitions.name: ScheduleWakeup
definitions.description:
Schedule a single self-paced wake. After 60–3600 seconds the given prompt is enqueued once into this session. On a daemon-hosted session the wake rides the session record (the daemon fires it, receipted, then it removes itself); on a bare streaming run it is a process-local timer that dies with the run.

This is the native way to run a self-paced loop: instead of a fixed cron cadence, you do a unit of work now and call ScheduleWakeup to wake yourself for the next unit. To continue the loop, the prompt you schedule should itself call ScheduleWakeup again when more work remains; to stop, simply don't reschedule.

## Input
- delaySeconds: how long to wait before the wake fires. Clamped to [60, 3600] seconds. Because the scheduler's resolution is one minute, the actual fire lands on the next minute boundary at or after the delay.
- prompt: the instruction to run when you wake.
- reason: optional short note on why you're waking yourself (for your own continuity; not shown to the user).

## When to use
- "check back in a few minutes once the build finishes" → delaySeconds: 120
- pacing a long self-directed task across several wakes without burning a turn idling
- Not for fixed recurring schedules ("every 5 minutes", "every day at 9am") — use CronCreate for those. This tool fires exactly once per call.

The wake fires only while the session is idle (not mid-turn), same as all scheduled prompts. When the operator interrupts or stops the session, the pending wake is dropped (with a receipt) and the loop does not resume on its own; a parked session keeps its wake and is woken by it when it fires.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds to wait before the wake fires. Clamped to [60, 3600]. The fire lands on the next minute boundary at/after the delay (cron resolution is 1 minute).

prompt.description: The prompt to enqueue when the wake fires.

reason.description: Optional short note on why you are waking yourself (for your own continuity; not shown to the user).

definitions.name: Monitor
definitions.description:
Use this over polling a log: new lines arrive as notifications while you keep working.

Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, indefinitely** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears", "wake me on every line another agent appends to this file") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`) and `persistent: true`, so the watch runs until you stop it with TaskStop or the session ends.
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run finishes") → Monitor with a command that exits when the watch is over.

A monitor without `persistent` expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 1 hour): it is killed and you get one expiry notice that says how to re-arm it. Lines that arrive within 200ms fold into one notification; ongoing output is delivered at most once every 30 seconds, with its line count and last line. Events that land while the session's usage window is closed are held by the watch and delivered together, in one notification, on your first turn after the window reopens — they are not lost, and they never wake a session the provider would refuse once the session has met the closed window.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms, min 1000ms, max 3600000ms; a value outside the bounds is clamped to them and the result says so. Ignored when persistent is true.

persistent.description: Run for the lifetime of the session (no timeout): the watch runs until TaskStop or the session ends. Use for session-length watches like PR monitoring, log tails or a file other agents append to.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

definitions.name: ContextLeft
RecordConvention
definitions.description:
Record one durable, user-stated project convention into the project instruction estate, so every future session here operates under it.

Use it the moment the user states a convention or a correction for this project — "always use bun here", "never touch the vendored dir", "tests run with the wrapper script". No magic word arms this; the statement itself does. Then say you recorded it and where.

The write follows the estate's own laws:
- The entry is MERCURY.md at the project root. A project without one gets a minimal entry born with the first rule.
- The pointer law: when MERCURY.md is a thin pointer at a fuller guide (an explicit @import), the rule lands in the pointed guide, never stacked into the pointer file. The tool follows the pointer for you and names the file it wrote.
- An exact restatement of an existing rule is a no-op (reported honestly). To merge — the user refined or corrected an existing rule — pass `replaces` with a distinctive substring of the old rule line, and the tool swaps that line in place wherever in the estate it lives.

Not for: one-off task details, session-scoped choices, a rule the user asks you to remember about how to work with them (pinned memory: Retain with pin, in their words), or private lessons about your own working method (your own memory, not the shared estate).

Deeper curation — folding several related rules into one, deleting stale lines — is ordinary editing: read the estate file and edit it directly.

rule.description: the durable project convention, as one plain standing-order sentence

replaces.description: merge verb: a distinctive substring of the existing rule line this one supersedes — the old line is swapped in place instead of a near-copy appended

definitions.name: Retain
definitions.description:
Store one or more durable facts into project memory.

- The response reports a per-item outcome: stored (with its id), already-staged (this session), or refused with the reason; a refused fact was not stored.
- One fact holds at most 2,000 characters, content and context together; a longer one is refused whole with its count, never cut — split it into facts under the limit. The disk holds exactly what the result says was stored; tell the user what was stored and what was refused, nothing more.
- Facts stage as pending observations and consolidate into topic pages automatically; they are recallable seconds after storing, labeled pending until consolidation.
- When the user asks you to remember a rule or a preference about how to work with them ("always …", "from now on …", "every session", "keep this as a rule"), store their words as said with pin: true — it is on the pinned shelf at once, loaded into every session, marked as asked for by the user, and never reworded, merged or dropped by Mercury. A plain "remember: <a fact>" is a fact, not a rule: store it without pin; the pin needs words that ask for a standing rule. This is the door for a remembered rule; a project convention about the code (how it is built, run or tested, what not to touch) goes to the instruction file, never here. Never pin on your own judgement.
- When the user says the new rule replaces an earlier one ("instead of …", "that replaces the old rule", a restatement after they unpinned the old rule in /memory), pass replaces: "seq:<n>" naming that rule — from the pinned shelf, or the unpinned rule the relevant memories show — so ONE rule stays current: the new rule takes its place and the old one is kept as history. Two rules that merely share words are not a conflict — both stay. Replacing a rule marked asked for by the user puts one yes/no card to the user with the rule's words and its replacement; No keeps the rule. Under the sovereign permission mode it is replaced without the card. A session with no one to answer the card refuses: tell the user the road — in /memory, under pinned rules, ↵ opens the rule and c corrects it (u unpins it).
- A fact that states the opposite of one already on record (always against never, on against off, a negation, a differing number) is refused whole, naming the record it conflicts with; nothing is stored beside its opposite. A contradiction is the user's call: tell them the conflict in one line and ask which is true; never Correct the record on a contradiction refusal without their word in the same conversation. On their word, Correct the old one with their reason and retain again, or retain both with the difference stated (when, where, which); a pinned rule is the user's to change, the road is in /memory.
- Only when the user asks for something to be remembered: a preference about how to work, a constraint they state, a fact they name — in their words. Never on your own judgement; a decision or an outcome belongs in the project's records, not in memory. The tool refuses a write when the user's latest message does not ask for something to be remembered ("remember …", "don't forget …", "note this down", "from now on …", "pin this"), and a crewmate's write always: a crewmate's finding goes in its report. Not for: secrets, transcripts, or anything the repo already records. A fact that looks like a key, a token or a password is refused by the tool itself, whoever asked: memory is a plain-text record on disk.

context.description: Where the fact came from (provenance note).

pin.description: Only when the user asked to remember this as a standing rule or preference: pins it, in their words, marked as asked for by the user. A pin needs the user's own words in the main chat — the rule in their latest message, or their 'yes, pin it' after stating it; otherwise it is refused and nothing is stored. A crewmate cannot pin: retain the fact without pin.

replaces.description: Only when the user said this rule replaces an earlier one: that rule as seq:<n> — from the pinned shelf, or the rule the user unpinned in /memory and now restates. The new rule takes its place and the old one becomes history, so one rule stays current. For a rule marked asked for by the user, the user answers a yes/no card first (under sovereign, no card).

definitions.name: Recall
definitions.description:
Search project memory for pointers, or read one full record.

- `query` — words, paths and topic names match. The answer is at most 20 pointers, each: a stable id (seq:<n> for a fact or ruling, pending:<ts> for a staged row, ledger:<ordinal> for a session or its handoff), a kind (fact · ruling · handoff · session), a one-line title (where it lives, when, from whom, which of your words matched) and footnotes (the session it came from, the ruling it fell under, what it supersedes or was superseded by).
- `read` — one entry with its breadcrumb and footnotes (doc:<slug> reads the whole page); a ledger read shows the session's entry and its handoff verbatim ("no note left" when none). Correct amends a record only after a full read.
- A pointer carries no content: open the record with read before you rely on it or quote it. Follow a footnote by reading the id it names.
- An empty result is flagged elidable — treat it as droppable context, not an error.
- Recall never writes anything.

query.description: Search memory for pointers: facts and pinned rulings in the pages, archive and pending observations, and the sessions and handoffs of the lineage ledger. A phrase or regex matches literally; otherwise the words of the query are matched. A pointer is an id, a title and footnotes: open one with read to see the record.

read.description: Read one full record by id: seq:<n> (a fact or ruling) · doc:<slug> (a whole page) · pending:<ts> · ledger:<ordinal> (a session's entry and its handoff).

definitions.name: Reflect
definitions.description:
Answer a question by synthesizing over recalled memory, with citations.

- Runs a Recall for your query, then one bounded model call over the hits. The synthesis cites the records it uses ([seq N] / [pending N]); a synthesis that cites nothing or invents ids is refused and the raw recall returned instead — grounding is structural, not advisory.
- No usable model/credentials degrades typed: you get the raw recall plus the reason.
- This costs a model call — use Recall alone when you just need the records. Reflect never writes anything.

query.description: The question to answer over memory.

definitions.name: Correct
definitions.description:
Correct one memory record by its id from Recall.

- Only when the user asks for a memory to be remembered or changed, in their words ("remember: … instead of …", "update the note about …"). Never on your own judgement: a change said in passing is not an ask. The tool refuses a change when the user's latest message does not ask for a memory to be remembered or changed (a pinned rule the user asked for goes to its card instead, as below), and a crewmate's always: a crewmate's finding goes in its report.
- op 'supersede' — a new truth replaces the fact; pass content (or replacementId naming an existing seq that already carries the truth). The old fact moves to history with a superseded-by pointer.
- op 'amend' — fix the record's own wording; requires the full record to have been read this session (Recall read:"<id>" first) so a clipped preview can never destroy an unseen tail.
- op 'retract' — mark the fact wrong with a reason. A consolidated fact is never hard-deleted: history is the audit spine.
- A pending row (pending:<ts>) is a draft, not yet a fact: retract strikes it — its bytes leave the buffer and no history is kept; supersede or amend replaces it with a new pending row, and the new row keeps the old words as its history until consolidation files the fact. This is the road when the user asks to correct or forget something said minutes ago, before consolidation. A corrected or struck draft never lands on a page.
- A pinned rule marked "asked for by the user" changes only on the user's answer: the tool puts one card to them with the rule's words as stored and what will happen. Yes runs the op as /memory does (the old wording to history; a draft struck); No returns "the user kept the rule" and nothing changes. Under the sovereign permission mode the op runs without the card and its record says so. A session with no one to answer the card refuses: tell the user the road — in /memory, under pinned rules, ↵ opens the rule and c corrects it (the old wording goes to history), u unpins it. A rule they have unpinned is a plain fact again and Retain with replaces supersedes it when they restate it.
- Content that looks like a key, a token or a password is refused: memory never holds a secret.

op.description: supersede = new truth; amend = fix wording (read the full record first); retract = mark wrong (a consolidated row keeps its history; a pending row is a draft and is struck).

id.description: The record id from Recall: seq:<n> for a consolidated row, pending:<ts> for a draft still in the buffer.

replacementId.description: supersede only: an existing seq:<n> already carrying the truth.

reason.description: Why — corrections always carry their reason.

definitions.name: Journal
definitions.description:
Write a brief entry into the journal: where the project is, what the queued backlog is, and what the user asked for in this session, in their words — never Mercury's own standing instructions. Plain words, concise, no longer than a sentence.

- One entry per session; a later call replaces the earlier one. The entry is written to the journal when this session ends. The journal lives in the Mercury home beside the project's memory, never under the project tree, and Mercury never pushes, syncs or shares it. The next session reads the last entry only when the operator's setting (memory.journalOnEntryPage) says so; the operator reads it in /memory.
- The rules Mercury itself works under (its git rules, its constitution) are not the user's constraints: write down only what the user said in this session.

entry.description: A brief entry: where the project is, what the queued backlog is, and what the user asked for in this session, in their words — never Mercury's own standing instructions. Plain words, concise, no longer than a sentence. Under 4000 characters.

definitions.name: ListMcpResources
definitions.description:
Survey the resources your connected MCP servers publish.
Each row names its providing server in a 'server' field, beside the protocol-defined resource fields (uri, name, and optionally mimeType and description).

server.description: Restrict the listing to one server, by name

definitions.name: ReadMcpResource
definitions.description: Read a single resource from a connected MCP server. The result carries the resource contents as returned by the server (text, or a note about where binary content was saved).

server.description: The name of the MCP server to read the resource from

uri.description: The URI of the resource to read

definitions.name: ToolSearch
definitions.description:
Load the full schemas of deferred tools so they become callable.

Deferred tools are listed in <system-reminder> messages that begin "Deferred tools:", one per line: the name, then what the tool is for. Before that fetch, the name and its line are all you hold — without a parameter schema the tool stays uncallable. Hand it a query; it matches against the deferred roster and admits each match: the result names the admitted tools, and from that request on their complete definitions are in your tool list, no different from the tools the prompt opened with. A tool already in your tool list needs no fetch: call it directly. A select that names a tool this session does not have loads nothing; the result names the miss.

Query forms:
- `select:WebFetch,Sleep` — names spelled as the list spells them
- `notebook jupyter` — keyword search
- `+slack send` — "slack" must appear in the name; remaining terms only rank

query.description: What to load: exact names as "select:<name>,<name>", or keywords ranked against the deferred roster.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)
